title: Cabinet raises rabi fertiliser subsidy 64% to Rs 62,370 crore as global prices climb
dek: The Centre will pay more to keep DAP and other phosphatic and potassic fertilisers affordable for the winter crop, citing the West Asia crisis and the Russia-Ukraine war.
author: Declaration Desk
body:
The Union Cabinet has approved subsidy rates for phosphatic and potassic (P&K) fertilisers for the 2026-27 rabi season at an estimated cost of Rs 62,370.02 crore, about 64% more than last year, to keep prices for farmers steady as international fertiliser costs rise.

The decision, taken at a meeting chaired by Prime Minister Narendra Modi on Wednesday, covers the season from 1 October 2026 to 31 March 2027, so it applies retrospectively from the start of the month in which rabi sowing began. The government said the cost was tentative. For rabi 2025-26 the budgeted figure was Rs 37,952.29 crore, which means an increase of about Rs 24,418 crore.

## What the Cabinet approved

The subsidy is paid under the Nutrient Based Subsidy (NBS) scheme, which has run since 1 April 2010. Under it, the government fixes a subsidy per kilogram of each nutrient (nitrogen, phosphorus, potash and sulphur), and pays it to manufacturers and importers, who in turn sell to farmers at lower prices. The new rates cover 28 grades of P&K fertilisers, including di-ammonium phosphate (DAP), the most widely used phosphatic fertiliser, and NPK complex fertilisers.

According to the government's release, the rates were set "in view of recent trends in international prices" of urea, DAP, muriate of potash (MOP) and sulphur. "Availability of fertilizers to farmers at subsidized, affordable and reasonable prices will be ensured," it said.

Reports of the Cabinet briefing put the new per-kilogram rates at Rs 94.21 for nitrogen, Rs 66.11 for phosphorus, Rs 2.38 for potash and Rs 10.42 for sulphur, and said the retail price of DAP would stay at Rs 1,350 for a 50-kg bag through a special provision on top of the NBS rate. These figures were not in the release.

## Why the bill has grown

Information and Broadcasting Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw, briefing reporters, blamed the conflict in West Asia and the Russia-Ukraine war for the rise in prices. "The Modi government has provided a shield to farmers from geopolitical turmoil," he said, according to reports. "The government has protected farmers' interests by providing an adequate fertiliser subsidy."

India imports much of its DAP and almost all of its potash, which leaves the subsidy bill exposed to world prices. Mr Vaishnaw said stocks stood at about 23.5 million tonnes against an estimated rabi requirement of about 35 million tonnes, according to reports. One report put stocks of urea at 10.31 million tonnes and DAP at 2.86 million tonnes, both higher than a year earlier.

The higher rabi bill adds to pressure on the year's fertiliser budget, which may need a supplementary allocation, reports said.

## Other Cabinet decisions

The Cabinet also extended the Credit Guarantee Fund for Micro Units, which backs loans under the PM Mudra Yojana, to March 2031 with a corpus of Rs 5,000 crore. The government said Mudra had sanctioned 60.36 crore loans worth Rs 43.34 lakh crore up to September 2026. It extended the Stand-Up India scheme for women and Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe entrepreneurs to 31 March 2031, and approved Rs 3,230 crore for the Yuge Yugeen Bharat national museum in North and South Block in New Delhi, to be built in phases until 2030-31.

## What happens next

The new rates apply to sales from 1 October. Rabi sowing of wheat, pulses, mustard and other crops is under way.
